I am sixty this year, and I have been farming these fields in Quzhou County for more than thirty-five years. After graduating from the county agricultural technical school in the 1980s, I have always tried to balance what the books say with what my own eyes tell me. My husband and I manage eight mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. Our son and daughter work in Shijiazhuang now, so day-to-day it is just the two of us, though they come back for the hectic wheat harvest and maize sowing window in early June.

It is early March, and my winter wheat—Jimai22, an improved variety I have trusted for years—is greening up nicely after a snowy winter. I rotary-tilled the field last October before sowing, which is the standard here. This spring I will irrigate three times: at green-up in mid-March, at jointing in late April, and at grain-filling in mid-May. At jointing I will topdress with urea, bringing my total nitrogen for the wheat to about 18 kg per mu. I already put down compound fertilizer in the fall, so my phosphorus and potassium are basically set at 6 kg and 4 kg per mu respectively. I will spray herbicide once before the wheat gets too tall, and I will watch for aphids and powdery mildew—probably two more sprays, so three pesticide applications in total. I am targeting about 480 kg per mu for the wheat; I could chase higher yields with more fertilizer, but I have seen neighbors lodge their crop by overdoing it, and at my age I prefer steady, reliable income over gambling.

After wheat harvest in early June, the turnaround is brutally tight—sometimes only five to seven days. I will sow Denghai605, the hybrid maize everyone around here uses, with no-tillage directly into the wheat stubble. There is simply no time to plough, and skipping tillage saves water and diesel. I will apply compound fertilizer with the planter and side-dress urea at the V6 stage, aiming for 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu. Two irrigations should be enough for maize: one right after sowing if the soil is dry, and the crucial one at tasseling in late July or early August. I will spray herbicide once and watch for corn borers and armyworms, giving maybe two insecticide sprays, so three pesticide applications total. If the summer rains cooperate, I expect around 520 kg per mu from the maize.

I stick with the wheat-maize double crop because it is my insurance policy. If one crop has a bad year, the other usually carries us through. I know the science, but I also know that in Quzhou, groundwater is getting expensive and labor is scarce, so I keep my inputs efficient rather than maximal.
